summary: This unit teaches you to communicate as the person leading electrical work: briefing a team, giving and checking instructions, controlling switching by radio, planning and announcing power outages, explaining test results to customers in plain words, and dealing with other trades, suppliers, designers and inspectors. You will learn to choose the right channel, put the important things in writing, refuse unsafe requests politely, and make sure every message has been understood.

blocks.p: In electrical work a misunderstood message can kill: a circuit switched on while someone is still working on it, the wrong breaker opened, a warning that never reached the night shift. Poor communication also costs money: extra work done without agreement, the wrong cable delivered, a client who was never told the power would be off. At Level 3 you are the link between your team, the client, the other trades and the people who design and inspect the work. This unit is about doing that well.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Choose the right way to communicate
Decide when to speak face to face, phone, use the radio, send a message or email, or put it in a formal document, and keep a record of what matters.
Listen and check understanding
Listen actively, ask open questions, have people repeat back or show you, and notice body language.
Overcome barriers
Deal with noise, distance, language, hearing, reading difficulty, shyness and stress, and include every member of the team.
Brief and instruct a team
Give job briefings and toolbox talks, write clear instructions, demonstrate tasks, and give and take feedback.
Communicate for safe switching
Use locks, tags, permits, signs and agreed radio messages so that nothing is switched until everyone is confirmed clear.
Plan and announce outages
Agree the time, give written notice, confirm, and keep people informed if the plan changes.
Deal with customers
Explain findings and risks in plain words, confirm them in writing, handle complaints, agree changes in writing and refuse unsafe requests.
Work with others on site
Take part in site meetings, raise queries, deal with suppliers, other trades and inspectors, and escalate problems you cannot solve.
Write and record
Write notes, emails, notices and site diary entries that are accurate, polite and complete, and keep clients' information confidential.

blocks.note: On Jamaican sites most of the team talk in Patois, and that is fine among people who share it. Written records, notices and messages to clients, designers and inspectors are in Standard English, and you switch to clear Standard English whenever someone in the conversation may not follow Patois, such as a visiting engineer or a hotel guest.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: How communication works, and choosing the channel

blocks.p: Every message has a **sender**, a **message**, a **channel** (the way it is sent) and a **receiver**. It is only complete when **feedback** comes back that shows the receiver understood it as the sender meant it. Most failures happen because the sender assumed the message had arrived.

flow: Decide what the other person needs to know or do
Choose the channel
Send a clear, complete message
Get feedback: repeat-back, a reply, or the action itself
Record it if it matters

head: Channel
Good for
Weak points
rows: Face to face
Briefings, explaining faults, bad news, sorting out disagreements; you can see whether the person understands
No record unless you write it down
Phone call
Urgent matters; quick answers
No record; easy to mishear figures
Two-way radio
Switching and testing with people out of sight
One person talks at a time; noise; others share the channel
Text or messaging app
Short confirmations, photos, arrival times
Easy to misread; may not be seen; not for formal agreements
Email
Anything that needs a record: confirmations, queries, reports, quotations
Slow for urgent matters; may not be read
Formal documents
Outage notices, permits, variations, certificates, incident reports, minutes
Take time to prepare
Drawings, sketches, marked-up plans
Positions, routes, connections
Need to be kept up to date
Signs, tags and labels
Warnings that must stay in place when you are gone
Only work if they are clear and in the right place

ul: **Urgent and safety-critical:** speak, then confirm in writing.
**Money, changes and safety defects:** always in writing.
**Positions and routes:** show, do not just tell. Walking round with a marked plan and tape marks on the walls beats any phone description.
If a written message about something important gets no reply, **follow up** by phone and note that you did.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: ETA
Estimated time of arrival: 'Delivery ETA 2 p.m.'
CC / BCC
Copy / blind copy: an address in BCC gets the email without the other receivers seeing that address
RFI
Request for information: a written query to the designer
O&M manual
Operation and maintenance manual, handed to the client at the end of a job
GCT
General Consumption Tax, added to quotations and invoices in Jamaica
FFL
Finished floor level: heights on drawings are measured from it

sections.title: Listening, questioning, body language and barriers

ul: Stop what you are doing and face the speaker.
Let them finish. Do not plan your reply while they talk.
Show that you are following: nod, say 'yes', 'go on'.
Repeat the key points back in your own words: 'So the breaker trips only when the pump starts?'
Write down figures, names, times and anything you have promised.

head: Type
Example
Use
rows: Closed (answered yes or no)
'Is the main switch locked off?'
To confirm one fact
Open (needs a full answer)
'What happens just before it trips?'
To find out what you do not know
Checking (the person shows or explains)
'Show me where the strappers go.' 'Talk me through how you will prove it dead.'
To check that an instruction was understood
Leading (suggests the answer)
'That makes sense, doesn't it?'
Avoid: people just agree

blocks.note: **'Do you understand?' is the weakest check there is.** Most people say yes, especially a new or shy trainee in front of others. Ask them to tell you back the main points, or to show you the first step, and watch the first part of the work.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Helps
Harms
rows: Calm, steady voice
Shouting, sighing, mumbling
Eye contact; facing the person
Looking at your phone or the floor
Open stance, a comfortable distance
Folded arms; standing over or too close to someone
Tidy appearance, ID worn in a client's home
Walking in without greeting anyone

blocks.h: Barriers and how to get past them

head: Barrier
What to do
rows: Noise (plant rooms, generators, grinders)
Move somewhere quieter to give the instruction, then check back; use agreed hand signals where needed
Distance and being out of sight
Radio or phone with agreed messages; never shout switching instructions
Jargon
Plain words for customers; explain a term once
Different first language
Short sentences, drawings, gestures, check back often; agree key safety words; ask a person who speaks both languages to help
Hearing difficulty
Ask the person what helps; face them; write the key points
Difficulty with reading
Explain face to face and show on the drawing or the job, privately; use pictures and marked drawings
Shyness or fear of looking foolish
Ask open questions one to one; thank people for asking
Anger, stress and tiredness
Stay calm, listen first, deal with facts, take a break if needed
Poor signal or flat radio batteries
Check equipment before the job; agree what to do if contact is lost

blocks.p: **Inclusion** means that every member of the team gets the message in a way that works for them, without being singled out or embarrassed. Never leave someone out of a briefing because it takes more effort to include them. Treat everyone with the same respect, whatever their age, gender, religion, background or position.

sections.title: Leading the team: briefings, instructions, training and feedback

blocks.p: Give the briefing at the work area, with the drawings and the method statement in your hand, before any tool is lifted.

flow: The job: what we are doing today and why
Tasks: who does what
Hazards and controls
Isolation points, locks and tags
How we will communicate, and who gives the order to switch
Emergencies: first aider, isolator, nearest phone
Questions, then each person tells back their task

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk, about ten minutes, given to the team at the start of a job or shift. Keep it to one topic that matters today, use a real example, and get the team talking rather than lecturing them. 'Same as yesterday' is not a briefing.

head: Vague
Clear
rows: Sort out Room 3 when you can.
Fix four outlet boxes in Room 3, 300 mm above FFL, at the positions marked in red on drawing E-04. Finish by 3 p.m.
Wire up the lights as usual.
Wire circuit 6 (corridor lights) in 2.5 mm² from DB-1 way 6. Do not connect at the board: I will check first.

blocks.p: A good instruction says **what, where, how many, to what standard, by when**, and what to do if there is a problem. Before installing unfamiliar equipment, read the **maker's installation manual**: it gives the wiring, clearances and safety warnings that no delivery note or price list will.

blocks.h: Job cards and what you find on site

blocks.p: A job card tells you what the client asked for. If you find something different, such as a burnt lampholder behind 'three failed lamps', do not just do what the card says and do not quietly do extra work. **Make it safe, tell the client what you found, and agree the extra work** before you do it.

flow: Explain what the task is for and its dangers
Show it at normal speed, then slowly, saying each step
Let the trainee try while you watch
Check, correct and praise what was right
Let them practise, and check again later

ul: Give it soon, and in private if it is a correction.
Be specific and balanced: 'Neat layout, but two terminals are loose. Check every one with the torque screwdriver.'
Talk about the work, not the person.
Say what to do next, and check later that it was done.
Do not take the job away and do it yourself: the trainee learns nothing.

blocks.p: When an inspector, a client or your supervisor finds fault with your team's work, listen without arguing, write down each point, ask about anything that is unclear, fix the defects and confirm that they are done. An inspector's list is free advice on how to make the installation safe.

blocks.h: Handing work over to someone else

ul: **Walk through the job together** at the work area.
Give a **written note**: what is finished, what is not, **what is live and what is isolated**, what is locked and by whom, and what must be tested before switching on.
Deal with the locks: the person taking over **fits their own lock before** you remove yours, so the isolation is never left unlocked.
Never leave covers off as a 'message'. Leave the work safe.

sections.title: Communication for safe isolation and switching

blocks.p: The rules of safe isolation are covered in your safety units. This section is about the messages that make them work when more than one person is involved.

ul: **Each person fits their own padlock** and removes only their own. One lock held by the senior person does not protect anyone else, and a spoken 'it's off' protects nobody.
A **danger tag** is fixed with each lock. It gives the worker's **name, the date and the reason**, and how to reach them. A board left isolated overnight must carry one.

A **permit-to-work** is a written authority used on larger sites. It records **who may work on what, under which controls**, for how long, and it is signed off when the work is finished. It does not replace locks and tags.
An **isolation procedure** is the written, step-by-step method for switching off, locking off and proving a piece of equipment dead.
Signs must be short and unmistakable: '**Danger: electrical. Authorised staff only**' on a switch room door; 'Danger: do not switch on. Persons working' at an isolator.

blocks.p: When the person at the board and the person at the equipment cannot see each other, agreed radio (or phone) procedure stops the two worst mistakes: switching the wrong circuit, and switching while someone is still in contact.

ul: Check radios, batteries and the channel before starting.
Start each message with who you are calling and who you are.
Say exactly **which circuit** and **what action**: 'Ready to switch ON circuit 7, Room 4 lights.'
The receiver **repeats the key part back** and says whether they are clear.
**Nothing is switched until the reply is heard.** No reply means no switching: go and find the person.
Keep messages short and use agreed words, so there is no doubt about what is being switched.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Roger
I have received and understood your message
Say again
Repeat your last message
Stand by
Wait: I will call you back
Go ahead
Carry out the action, or send your message
Over / Out
I have finished and expect a reply / the conversation is finished

blocks.p: **Example.** 'Andrew, this is Camille at DB-2. Ready to switch ON circuit 9, workshop outlets. Are you clear? Over.' 'Camille, Andrew. Circuit 9, workshop outlets. I am clear. Go ahead. Over.' Camille switches on. 'Circuit 9 is ON. Over.' 'Circuit 9 ON, outlets live. Out.'

blocks.note: 'Roger' on its own is not enough before switching. It says the message was heard; it does not say which circuit, or that the person is clear. Insist on the read-back.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Work complete, tested, tools out, covers on
Each person confirms by name that they are clear
Each person removes their own lock and tag
The one person in charge announces the switch-on
Switch on, check each circuit, and record the time

blocks.p: If someone collapses after a shock, the supply is cut first; then the first message is a **call for emergency help with the exact location**. In Jamaica, dial **110** for an ambulance or the fire brigade and 119 for the police. Give the address and a landmark, say what has happened and whether the person is breathing, and send someone to the gate to meet the ambulance. Messages to the client and the site diary come afterwards.
A planned outage is one you arrange in order to work safely. Handled well, it costs the client little. Handled badly, it loses them stock, data and customers, and loses you the client.

flow: Agree the date and time with the manager, choosing the time that affects the business least
Ask what depends on power: computers and servers, fridges and freezers, alarms, phones, card machines, medical or other special equipment
Give a written outage notice well in advance, at least several days
Tell anyone outside who is affected, such as the alarm monitoring company
Confirm by phone the day before
On the day: tell the manager when the power goes off and when it is back, and ask them to check their equipment
If the work will run late, tell them at once, with the reason and a new time
Record the off and on times in the site diary

head: Item
Example
rows: Date and day
Saturday 14 November 2026
Start and finish times
8:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon
What will be off
All lights, outlets, air-conditioning, the alarm panel and the card machines
Why
Replacement of the distribution board
What to do before
Save work and shut down computers by 7:45 a.m.; move chilled stock to the back fridge, which will stay on
What to do after
Wait for the all-clear from the electrician before switching equipment back on
Contact
A name and phone number

blocks.p: Listing the equipment that will lose power lets people save their work and protect what needs protecting. It also brings out things you did not know about, such as a fridge of medicines or a server that takes an hour to shut down.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican businesses have a standby generator or a UPS. Ask about them when you plan the outage: they keep fridges and computers running, but they are also sources of supply that must be isolated before you work.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Instead of
Say
rows: 'It is a residual current device rated at 30 mA.'
'It switches off very fast if current leaks, to help stop someone getting a shock.'
'The CPC is open circuit on two circuits.'
'Two circuits have no earth wire connected. The earth wire is the safety path that makes the breaker trip if something goes wrong.'
'IR is 0.3 MΩ on circuit 5.'
'The covering on the wires of the verandah lights is letting current leak, most likely because water is getting into a fitting.'

blocks.p: When tests show a safety problem, **explain the risk simply, and confirm it in writing, with options**. Do not hide it so that the customer is not worried, and do not frighten them into work they may not need. Say how serious it is, what you recommend, roughly what it will cost, and what they should do in the meantime. Then send a short written summary the same day, with the test results attached, and keep a copy.

A message that confirms a visit gives the **day, time, how long, and what you need**: 'Tuesday 17 November, 9 a.m., about one hour; we will need access to the roof.' 'Sometime next week' is not an appointment.

flow: Listen without interrupting
Apologise for the trouble
Explain what happened, honestly
Say what you will do, and by when
Do it, then check the customer is satisfied
Record it and tell your supervisor

blocks.p: Do not argue, blame other trades or tell the customer they should have read the notice. An honest explanation and a quick fix keep most customers.

ul: A **quotation** is your written price for stated work, showing GCT.

A **variation** is a change to the agreed work, such as extra outlets, that is priced and agreed separately. **Agree it in writing before doing it**: say thank you, note exactly what is wanted, check it with your supervisor and the designer if it affects the design, price it, and get the client's signature.
Changes agreed only by word of mouth are forgotten or remembered differently, the person asking may have no authority to spend, and payment is argued over later.
Record approved variations in the site diary and mark them on the drawings for the as-built record.
An **invoice** is the written request for payment after the work is done.

blocks.p: A customer, or even a supervisor, may ask you to bypass an RCD or GFCI, tape up a broken outlet, fit a bigger breaker or energise something untested. The answer is no, however politely they ask and however senior they are.

flow: Stay calm and polite
Say clearly that you cannot do it
Explain the danger in plain words
Offer a safe alternative, such as finding the fault or isolating one item
If they insist, do not do it
Write down what was said and report it to your supervisor

ul: Walk round together. Show the main switch and the board, how to read the circuit chart, how to switch off a circuit, and **how and when to test the RCDs or GFCIs** with the test button.
Hand over the documents: test results and certificate, as-built drawings, circuit chart, makers' instructions and warranties, ideally in an O&M file.
Agree a **snag list**: the items not finished or needing correction, with dates.
Explain what to do if a breaker trips, and who to call.
Ask the client to sign that the handover was done, and keep a copy.

blocks.p: You see inside people's homes and businesses: their alarm systems, safes, cameras, stock and routines. That information is **confidential**. If a neighbour, a friend or another client asks about a job, politely say that you cannot discuss a client's work. Do not post photos of a client's property online, and keep drawings and reports where others cannot read them.

If you notice a danger outside your job, such as a badly corroded earth rod connection, a hot breaker or a damaged service cable, **tell the owner and put it in writing** on your report. If it is urgent, make it safe first. Saying nothing because 'it was not my job' leaves people at risk; quietly fixing it leaves no record.

sections.title: Other trades, suppliers, designers and inspectors

ul: Bring a short written progress list: work done, problems, what you need from others and by when.
**Raise problems at the meeting**, with the facts and the risk: a water tank planned above your main board, ceilings to be closed before the wiring is inspected.
Make sure each decision is **recorded in the minutes** with an owner and a date. What is not minuted is easily denied.
Listen to the other trades' problems too: the programme only works if the trades fit together.
Tell your team afterwards what was agreed.

blocks.p: If the drawings are unclear, wrong or silent, do not guess and do not ask another trade. Send a **written query** (an RFI) to the designer through the main contractor, with a marked-up drawing or photo, and keep the answer. A guessed board position that turns out wrong is rebuilt at your cost.

ul: Order in writing, with the full description: type, size, rating, quantity and delivery date.
Ask for an ETA and tell the site when to expect the delivery.
If a supplier offers a **substitute**, such as 4 mm² cable in place of 6 mm², do not accept it without the **designer's written approval**. A different size or type can break the design.
Check deliveries against the order before signing for them.

flow: Talk to the other team leader early, calmly and in person
Listen to what they need; explain what you need, with the drawings
Look for a fair plan: who goes first, which area, which hours
Agree how you will keep each other informed
Write it in the site diary and tell your team
If you cannot agree, take it to the site manager with the facts

blocks.p: Do not move another trade's materials or work, do not retaliate, and do not complain to the client first. Most clashes are settled in five minutes by two people looking at the same drawing.

**Escalation** means passing a problem you cannot solve up to a more senior person: a clash you cannot settle, a client who will not act on a danger, an instruction you believe is unsafe. Escalate early, with the facts and what you have already tried. It is part of the job, not a failure.

ul: Before an electrical inspector's visit, prepare the **test results, drawings and certificates**, and make sure there is safe **access** to the work.
Have a competent person there who knows the job.
Answer questions honestly. If you do not know, say so and find out.
Treat the inspector as you would any professional: no arguments, and never a gift or favour.
Note each defect, fix it, and confirm in writing when it is done.

blocks.p: When a trainee reports a hot breaker, a smell of burning or a near miss, thank them, make the situation safe and report it to the client or the site manager. A near miss, such as a drill that just missed a hidden cable, is reported so that the cause can be fixed before someone is hurt, never to punish the person who reported it. A team that is thanked for reporting keeps reporting.

The **site diary** is the daily written record of work done, people on site, visitors, instructions received, deliveries, weather and problems. Note the **time each circuit or board was switched off and on**: if a client later claims that stock was spoiled or a machine was damaged, the diary is your evidence.

ul: A subject line that says what it is about: 'Power off Sat 14 Nov, 8 a.m. to 12 noon: board replacement'.
A greeting, then the main point in the first two lines.
Short paragraphs or a short list; dates, times and figures written in full.
Say clearly what you want the reader to do, and by when.
Check attachments are attached, and names and figures are right, before you send.
Use CC for people who need to know, and BCC when receivers should not see each other's addresses.
Polite and plain: no slang, no capitals for shouting.
Good for short, factual messages and photos to your supervisor.
Photos of a fault are most useful as **clear close-ups, with the location and the circuit** written in the message.
Voice notes leave nothing to search or print: put figures and instructions in writing.
Never send a client's details or photos to a public group or social media.
Anything that changes the price, the design or safety is confirmed by email or on a form.

head: Weak
Strong
rows: Circuit 4 is kind of bad, I think.
Circuit 4 (kitchen outlets) fails the insulation test: 0.2 MΩ. It has been isolated and tagged.
Everything was tested and some things were not great.
Of 12 circuits, 10 passed. Circuits 4 and 9 failed; details are below.

blocks.p: After an incident or near miss, the written report gives: the date, time and exact place; the people involved and witnesses; what happened, in order, as facts; what was done straight away; the injury or damage; the likely causes; and the actions to stop it happening again, with names and dates. It ends with the writer's name, signature and date. Your report-writing unit covers this in full.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can choose the right channel for a message and say when it must be in writing.
I can listen actively and check understanding with open questions, repeat-back and 'show me'.
I can name the common barriers to communication and get past each one.
I can include team members with different languages, hearing, reading skills and confidence.
I can give a job briefing and a toolbox talk.
I can write an instruction that says what, where, how many, to what standard and by when.
I can demonstrate a skill and give specific, balanced feedback.
I can hand a part-finished job over safely, in person and in writing.
I can manage locks, tags, permits and signs within a team.
I can use clear radio messages with read-back, and I do not switch without a reply.
I can plan an outage and write an outage notice.
I can explain test results and risks to a customer in plain words and confirm them in writing.
I can handle a complaint, a variation and an unsafe request.
I can hand over a finished job with its documents and a snag list.
I can raise issues at site meetings, send a query to the designer and deal with suppliers' substitutes.
I can settle a clash with another trade or escalate it with the facts.
I can prepare for an inspector's visit and respond to a list of defects.
I can keep a site diary and keep clients' information confidential.

terms: Giving a speaker your full attention and checking that you understood.
Blind copy: an email address the other receivers cannot see.
Describes information that must not be shared outside the job.
A label fixed with a lock to an isolator, giving the worker's name, the date and the reason.
Passing a problem you cannot solve up to a more senior person.
The reply or action that shows a message was understood; also, comments on someone's work.
The written request for payment sent after work is done.
The written steps for switching off, locking off and proving equipment dead.
The written record of a meeting: decisions, owners and dates.
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no.
A notice telling building users that the power will be off for a set time.
A written authority recording who may work on what, under which controls.
Repeating the key part of a message to show it was received correctly.
Request for information: a written query to the designer.
Radio word meaning 'I have received and understood your message'.
The daily written record of work, visitors, weather and problems on a site.
The list, agreed with the client, of items not finished or needing correction.
A short safety talk given to a team at the start of a job or shift.
A change to the agreed work that is priced and agreed separately.

c1.title: A board change at a Port Antonio print shop
c1.text: Team leader Kemoy Stewart will replace the old distribution board at a print shop in Port Antonio, Portland. The power will be off on Saturday 14 November 2026 from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon. The shop has computers holding customers' print jobs, large printers, a drinks fridge, card machines and an alarm that is watched by a monitoring company. Kemoy must tell the manager, Mrs Chin, and her eight staff.

c2.title: Switching checks at a Moneague high school
c2.text: At a high school in Moneague, St Ann, electrician Orane is at distribution board DB-3 and his partner Shamar is in classroom Block B, 80 m away and out of sight. They are switching on newly wired circuits one at a time and checking them, using two-way radios. Painters are also working in Block B.

c3.title: Test results for a homeowner in Stony Hill
c3.text: Mrs Pauline Edwards, a retired teacher, owns a 40-year-old house in Stony Hill, St Andrew. Electrician Damion Reid's tests show: no GFCI protection on the bathroom and kitchen outlets; an insulation resistance of 0.3 MΩ on the verandah lighting circuit, where rain gets into a fitting; and a bedroom outlet with a cracked face. She asks, 'Is my house going to burn down?' and then, 'Can't you just tape up that outlet for now?'

c4.title: A site meeting for apartments in Liguanea
c4.text: Team leader Simone Reid attends the weekly site meeting for a six-storey apartment block in Liguanea, St Andrew. The builder wants the 3rd-floor ceilings closed on Friday, but the electrical first fix there has not yet been inspected. The fire-alarm cable route on the drawings now clashes with a duct the air-conditioning installer has fitted, and his foreman is annoyed. The client's architect chairs the meeting.

c5.title: A shift handover at an Old Harbour feed mill
c5.text: At a feed mill in Old Harbour, St Catherine, day-shift electrician Rushane has half finished replacing a motor starter in panel MCC-2 when his shift ends at 4 p.m. Night-shift electrician Kadian will finish it. The incoming busbars in the panel are still live. The starter's outgoing circuit is isolated at switch Q4 and locked with Rushane's padlock and tag.

questions.q: Which wording is best for the main line of Kemoy's outage notice?
o: Electrical work will take place at the shop this weekend
Please note the power may go off at some point on Saturday
Power OFF Saturday 14 November, 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon
The electricians will need the building for a while soon
questions.why: A notice must give the exact day, date and start and finish times, so that people can plan. 'This weekend', 'at some point' and 'soon' leave the staff guessing and the computers unsaved.

questions.q: Apart from Mrs Chin and her staff, who most needs to be told about the outage before the day?
o: The alarm monitoring company
The JPS office, to cut the street supply
The shop's insurance company
The customers who are on the mailing list
questions.why: When the alarm panel loses power, the monitoring company may treat it as a fault or a break-in and send a response. Telling them in advance avoids a false call-out. The board is isolated at the shop's own main switch, so JPS is not involved.

questions.q: Which subject line is best for the email to Mrs Chin confirming the outage?
o: Hello from the electricians
Important!!! Please read this now
Power off Sat 14 Nov, 8 a.m.–12 noon: board change
Information about some upcoming electrical work at your shop
questions.why: A subject line should tell the reader what the email is about before it is opened, and make it easy to find later. The date, time and reason do that; greetings and exclamation marks do not.

questions.q: At 11:30 a.m. Kemoy sees that the job needs 90 minutes more than planned. What should he do?
o: Finish quietly, since 90 minutes is not long
Tell Mrs Chin now, with the reason and new time
Text the staff once the power is back on
Reconnect the old board and come back on another day
questions.why: People have planned around the time on the notice. Telling the manager at once, with the reason and a new time, lets her protect stock and tell staff and customers. Silence turns a small delay into a complaint.

questions.q: Orane calls: 'Shamar, Orane at DB-3. Ready to switch ON circuit 12, Block B outlets. Are you clear?' Which reply should Shamar give?
o: 'Roger that, go ahead and switch it whenever you are ready.'
'Yes man, everything good down here, you can go on.'
'Hold on a little, I think that is the one I am on.'
'Orane, Shamar. Circuit 12, Block B outlets. I am clear.'
questions.why: The read-back names the circuit and states that he is clear, so both know they mean the same circuit. 'Roger' and 'everything good' confirm only that something was heard, not what will be switched.

questions.q: Orane calls Shamar twice about the next circuit and hears no reply. What should he do?
o: Switch on, since Shamar knows the plan
Not switch, and go to find Shamar
Switch on and off quickly as a signal
Ask a painter to shout across to him
questions.why: No reply means no switching. Shamar may have a flat battery, or he may have his hands in the circuit. The only safe action is to leave the circuit off and make contact in person.

questions.q: During the checks Shamar says, 'Say again.' What does he want Orane to do?
o: Switch the same circuit on a second time
Speak in a louder voice from now on
Repeat his last message
Stop work and wait for him to call back
questions.why: 'Say again' is the agreed radio phrase for 'repeat your last message'. Agreed words keep messages short and remove doubt about what is meant.

questions.q: Which explanation of the verandah circuit's test result suits Mrs Edwards best?
o: Rain is getting into a verandah light, so current leaks
The IR on circuit 5 is 0.3 MΩ, below the minimum allowed
There is a line-to-earth insulation fault in the luminaire
The verandah lighting has failed its dead tests, I am afraid
questions.why: A customer needs the cause and the effect in everyday words. Readings, circuit numbers and trade terms belong in the written test results, which she can keep, not in the explanation.

questions.q: How should Damion answer her question, 'Is my house going to burn down?'
o: Tell her not to worry, as the house has lasted 40 years
Tell her yes, unless the whole house is rewired at once
Tell her he cannot say until she has paid for the tests
Explain the real risks calmly, and how to fix each
questions.why: The customer is owed the truth, in proportion: what the risks are, how serious each is and what can be done. Hiding the risk leaves her in danger; exaggerating it is dishonest pressure.

questions.q: What should Damion do about her request to 'just tape up' the cracked outlet?
o: Tape it neatly and warn her to be careful with it
Decline, explain why and offer to replace it
Tape it, but write that she insisted on it
Ignore the request and say nothing more
questions.why: Tape does not make a cracked outlet safe: live parts can still be reached. He refuses politely, explains the danger in plain words and offers the safe alternative: replace it now, or isolate it until it is replaced.

questions.q: What should Damion send Mrs Edwards on the same day as his visit?
o: A short written summary of findings and options
Nothing more, as he explained it all to her in person
Only the invoice for the inspection and testing work
The full schedule of readings, with no explanation
questions.why: A spoken explanation is soon forgotten or remembered differently. A short written summary, with the test results attached, lets her decide and shows later that she was told.

questions.q: What should Simone say about closing the 3rd-floor ceilings on Friday?
o: Nothing; she can cut access holes afterwards
That no trade may work on that floor until further notice
That it must wait for the inspection, and be minuted
That the builder must take the blame for any delay
questions.why: Wiring hidden before inspection may have to be exposed again at great cost. Raising it at the meeting, with the reason, and having the decision minuted, makes sure the programme allows for the inspection.

questions.q: How should the clash between the fire-alarm cable route and the new duct be settled?
o: Simone re-routes the cable her own way and marks up the drawing later
The trade that finishes first keeps its route
The duct is moved by her team after hours
A written query, with a marked drawing, goes to the designer
questions.why: A fire-alarm route is part of the design. A change needs the designer's decision, asked for in writing through the proper channel with a marked-up drawing or photo, so that the answer is on record.

questions.q: The air-conditioning foreman raises his voice and says his duct is staying where it is. What should Simone do first?
o: Stay calm, listen, and look at the drawing with him
Raise her own voice so that she is heard
Walk out and phone the client to complain
Tell her team to run the cable over the duct anyway
questions.why: Anger is a barrier: nothing is settled while voices are raised. Staying calm, listening and dealing with the facts on the drawing usually settles a clash; if not, it goes to the chair with the facts.

questions.q: After the meeting, which record best protects everyone?
o: Simone's own memory of what was agreed
Minutes listing each action, its owner and date
A voice note sent to her team that evening
A photo of all the people who were at the site meeting
questions.why: Minutes that name each action, who owns it and when it is due are the agreed record of the meeting. Memories differ, and a voice note to one team is not something the other parties have accepted.

questions.q: What should happen to the padlock on Q4 at the handover?
o: Rushane leaves his lock on and gives Kadian the key
Rushane removes his lock, and Kadian fits one later
Kadian fits his own lock, then Rushane removes his
Both locks stay off until Kadian is ready to start
questions.why: Each person is protected only by their own lock, and the isolation must never be left unlocked. The person taking over fits their lock and tag first; only then does the person leaving remove theirs.

questions.q: Which written handover note is safest?
o: Starter nearly done, you will see what is left to do.
MCC-2: watch yourself in there. Call me if any problem.
Starter job is half finished. All isolated. See you tomorrow.
MCC-2 busbars LIVE. Q4 off, locked. Control wiring to do.
questions.why: A handover note states exactly what is live, what is isolated and locked, and what remains to be done. 'All isolated' is false here, because the busbars are live, and vague notes leave the next person to find out the hard way.

questions.q: Which toolbox talk is most likely to change how a team works?
o: Ten minutes on one of today's hazards, with questions
A one-hour reading of the whole safety manual, once a month
A quick 'same as yesterday, be careful' at the gate
A notice pinned up for the team to read later
questions.why: A toolbox talk works when it is short, about a hazard the team will meet that day, and involves them through questions and their own examples. Long readings and unread notices change nothing.

questions.q: A visiting engineer from Canada asks a trainee about the day's work, and the trainee answers in fast Patois. What is the best advice for the trainee?
o: Carry on as before, since visitors should learn the local speech
Say nothing, and let the supervisor do the talking
Switch to clear Standard English and check he follows
Speak the same words again, but much louder
questions.why: The aim is to be understood. Patois is fine among people who share it, but with someone who may not follow it you switch to clear Standard English, in short sentences, and check that the message has landed.

questions.q: Which question best checks that an apprentice has understood the isolation steps you have just explained?
o: 'You understood all of that, didn't you?'
'Talk me through how you will prove it dead.'
'Is there anything at all that you did not follow?'
'Shall I go over the whole thing once more?'
questions.why: Asking the apprentice to explain or show the steps reveals what they actually understood. Questions that can be answered with yes or no usually get a polite 'yes', whatever the truth.
